notes: Baseline: one product-manager role reads the brief and writes the PRD and the decision log in one call.

The parent never emitted the decisions artifact (missing_artifact on all 6 scenarios, artifacts_present 0.5), because one 4000-token call ran out after the PRD, so the decision log now has its own role. The soul adds scheduling mechanisms every critique said were missing: protected non-meeting blocks, a gap ladder for focus blocks, deadlines with splitting and reachability checks, surfacing conflicts instead of resolving them silently, propose-then-confirm replans, and a user-defined day boundary. Scope is capped at about 12 points (the parent's was 27): calendar sync (L) and voice input (M) are deferred and the diff view is merged into replan.

Every critique names a case the parent PRD never considered (overlapping meetings, sleep and child pickup as protected blocks, focus blocks, deadlines that move to tomorrow), and the decision log was never emitted. Pipeline: a drafter writes the PRD, a red-team critic walks five archetype users through a morning plan and a mid-day change and also points out features to cut, a reviser writes the final PRD and flows within a 14-point budget, and a decision logger loops with a tool checker until every entry cites assumption ids and covers the key trade-offs. The goal is replan_quality, plan_feasibility and tradeoff_rationale, the lowest criteria (2.0–2.3).

This child reverses the parent's PRD-first flow. Decisions come first. A simulator runs concrete days against them and messages back the breakages. A scope cutter sizes the features, and only then is the PRD compiled from decisions, flows and scope. Motivation: tradeoff_rationale scored 2 and the decision log was never produced, and every scenario critique found mechanisms that broke when walked through on a real day (overlaps, cross-midnight, deadlines, focus blocks). Running simulations before writing should surface those breaks. A human role asks whether replans auto-apply or need confirmation, the question that matters most to sceptical and control-minded users, and the team proceeds on 'proposal + one-tap accept'.

Same two-role team, with the prompts rewritten against the critiques. All 8 critiques gave plan_feasibility 2 because the PRD's one generic example double-booked fixed meetings, called a 3-hour task 'missing duration', and replanned in ways that made things worse. The prompts now require short worked examples, one per archetype (no-structure student, interrupted parent, urgent insert, overlapping-meeting trap, night shift), written as time tables with a fixed-first, list-gaps, then-place self-check. The judge also counted 20 points against the parent's claimed 14 (noon calibration, cross-midnight, reminder and voice were committed in the text but missing from the table), so the PRD's table now has to list every first-release capability and everything else is deferred explicitly. The confirmation card no longer blocks the plan.

Structural change: the parent's examples double-booked fixed meetings, which a judge read as proof the scheduler was unsafe (plan_feasibility 2/5 in all 8 scenarios). The worked examples now come from a dedicated flow_writer (6 archetype days as strict time tables), a deterministic timeline_check tool finds every overlap, and a fixer repairs only what the checker flags (at most 2 rounds, stopping on ALL_OK). The PM keeps rules and an honest 5-feature table (about 11 points, everything committed is counted, because the judge sized the parent at 20 against a claimed 14). The soul is the same as c1's.

Radical change: the worked examples are no longer written by an LLM. A tool role (day_sim.py) holds a deterministic reference scheduler and replanner covering fixed/protected blocks, buffers, focus versus fragment placement, pull-forward into freed slots, deadline-priority yielding, the later pool, honest 'cannot fit' messages and cross-midnight days. It runs that code on 8 archetype days (meeting-dense, interrupted parent, deep-work researcher, night shift, no-structure student, urgent insert, overlapping-meeting trap, overloaded day) and emits a verified `flows` artifact plus a short rule summary. The cause is that every critique traced plan_feasibility 2/5 to the parent's hand-made examples double-booking meetings, and a 30B worker cannot be trusted with time arithmetic; the PM and logger now only write rules, scope and trade-offs that cite the cases, at zero extra LLM tokens for the examples.

Every critique gave plan_feasibility 2 because the parent's hand-made timetable double-booked meetings, and earlier children that added more LLM timetables did worse, so this PM writes no clock-time arithmetic at all. Instead it writes an 8-archetype scenario playbook in relative terms, covering the paths the judge found missing: a freed meeting slot used for the PRD, a new immovable event with fragment-only time and a tomorrow-morning fallback, an urgent insert with an optimism warning, restart-from-now, a night shift, the skeptic trap and an overloaded day. The judge counted 20 points against the parent's claimed 14 because commitments were scattered outside the table, so the table is now exactly 3 rows (7 points) and everything else is either a row's acceptance criterion or an explicit deferral. The decision log opens with an A1–A7 index and adds a 'what changes if users are meeting-heavy' line to every entry, because the critiques said the A-ids were undefined (the parent wrote 'A3?').

Code-generated examples (gen02_a1_child_3) were the only change that lifted plan_feasibility (2.75), but that child lost tradeoff_rationale because the A-ids were undefined and the PRD misquoted the flows. This child keeps the parent's PM and logger pair (tradeoff 3) and adds a zero-token tool, day_sim.py, which runs a reference scheduler and replanner on 8 archetype days and emits overlap-checked `flows` plus an `assumptions` table defining A1–A7. The flows exercise exactly the paths the critiques found missing: freed-slot pull-forward, an urgent insert taking priority with a +40% estimate, a sick-child pickup with fragments and a deadline check, restart-from-now, a night shift, the overlap trap and an honest 'cannot fit'. The PM may only cite flows by id and never writes clock times, and the feature table shrinks to 3 honest rows (about 7 points) against the 20 the judge counted for the parent.

Radical division of labour: a tester LLM writes 6 diverse test days as JSON (personas beyond the visible ones, each with one change), the code planner day_sim.py runs them (falling back to built-in archetypes when parsing fails) into overlap-checked `flows` and an `assumptions` table, and a single writer emits decisions first and then the PRD. The aim is the hidden-persona gate: every critique traced plan_feasibility 2 to hand-made timetables, and hard-coded examples only cover the visible personas. Writing decisions first means a token cut can no longer drop the trade-off log, and the team has 3 roles, one of them free.

Same 3-role topology, but the engine is rebuilt on the critique evidence. Sleep is now a protected block placed first, and the engine drops the course rather than the sleep (S9). Urgent inserts keep their +40% buffer and every deadline task reports remaining work and slack (S12, S4). The parent's 'pickup by 15:30' contradiction is fixed (S4), and there is a 10-minute transition before every appointment (S1/S5). A stated or visible-default energy window replaces 'earliest gap', with focus capped at 120 minutes (S11). All 8 built-in archetypes (meeting-dense, skeptic traps, night shift) now always run, where tester cases used to push them out, and the tester adds at most 2 unusual days. The writer must size every committed capability honestly (the judge counted 22 points against the 7 claimed) and must write concrete 'if A1 flips' changes.

Uses the rebuilt engine from c1 (protected sleep, urgent buffer kept, slack and remaining-work reports, transition buffers, energy window, a pickup-by-deadline fix). The LLM tester is dropped: its 3k tokens mostly pushed the persona archetypes out of the flows. In its place a persona advocate runs before the writer and walks 8 kinds of user through the code-made flows. The advocate writes a `personas` artifact (what each user fears, what is guaranteed, the residual doubt, and a concrete rule or decision fix), and the writer has to fold those fixes in. Every fit critique was a persona saying 'my day is not shown or not trusted' (persona_trust 2-3), so the hypothesis is that a cheaper and more targeted persona pass beats generating more test days.

Radical: no code planner and no clock-time timetables. Most fit critiques penalised specific contradictions inside hand-made or engine-made timetables (a pickup after the deadline, sleep missing, the urgent buffer cut to 10%), so this team commits to policies and dialogue-level flows, and the judge checks rules instead of arithmetic. A scoper drafts the decision log and an explicit cut list. A hostile persona panel then attacks it over a message channel, one persona at a time, including users the scoper did not think of, for up to 2 rounds. The final writer turns the surviving decisions into a PRD and `flows` written as user utterance → confirmation card / diff proposal scripts with relative durations only.

Cheap fix of the parent's two concrete failure sources. (1) The LLM tester is fired: its cases pushed the meeting-dense, skeptic and night-shift archetypes out of flows (S1/S2/S6/S9 said 'my day is never shown'), so all 8 built-in days always run, with engine bugs from the critiques fixed (pickup replaces the 17:00 one and starts so the child is reached by 15:30; urgent +40% buffer is never compressed; sleep is an in-plan protected block with drop-the-course; energy peak window; deadline tasks never split past the deadline; optionals step aside, shrink to half, avoid the last hour; slack and remaining-buffer reports after every replan). (2) The writer must add a persona guarantee matrix and concrete if-assumption-flips changes, and must keep the 3 features while explicitly deferring reminder/midday calibration/calendar import, since the honest-sizing children ballooned to 34 points.

Structural change aimed at the flat tradeoff_rationale (3 in every critique) and at plan_feasibility. One 9k-token writer is split in two. A decider writes only the decision log, and decision_lint.py (code) checks it: every entry has two or more options, a choice, valid A/Q ids, a concrete if-assumption-fails change (it rejects 'support later' / 'not designed for it' dodges, which the parent's D1/D11 used), a meeting-heavy flip and a points line, and all 12 required topics are covered; a failed check sends it back once. A PRD writer then works from a compact code-built decision index, not the full log, so it stays consistent at low token cost. The tester is fired and the fixed 8-archetype engine from c1 is reused.

Radical division of labour: code owns every part of the PRD that must agree with the engine, and LLMs write only judgement. assemble.py builds the feature table (3 features, 7 points, plus a deferred list with points), rules R1–R11 each citing the F-examples where the engine actually fired them, the example guide, a decision index and a consistency check. A decider writes the trade-off log and a narrator writes positioning, persona guarantees, goals, not-doing, the evening wrap-up and risks; the tool stitches these together. Evidence: the global gap and several critiques were internal contradictions (the claimed 7 points vs the engine's behaviour, shown plans contradicting stated rules, 'sleep protected' asserted with no mechanism), which a single LLM writer keeps reintroducing; the fixed 8-archetype engine from c1 is reused and the tester is fired.
